text: Right, everyone gets a job, so nobody can say the crown played favourites. Graham, you hold the Harvest Pile, since wheat people count carefully. Paddy, you collect the tax, and please be gentle with your neighbours. Silke, you read the I Ching, and the crown pays you five a year to tell us honestly what the heavens say.

Reina appoints her table jobs for the whole game: Graham Garner banks the Harvest Pile and pays out every harvest, Paddy Doyle collects the tax, and Silke Weber reads the I Ching card each year and keeps the population counter, for 5 a year from the crown. Silke shuffles the I Ching deck.

Storyteller's tip: every work owed at this table is the crown's to pay for, 520 in all. That's eight projects (the three palaces, the Wall above Province 1, the canals in Provinces 1, 5 and 6, and the Province 7 Reservoir), and only one can be built a year. Tax can be raised only on positive incomes.

Forty percent this year, friends. That's twenty-four from each of you, and you still keep more than you hand over. The crown pays for the Summer Palace on its own, and next year we start on the Wall and the canals.

Paddy collects the tax at 40%: 24 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 72 to the crown. Reina builds the Summer Palace on G20 in Province 1, paying the 20 herself; the Wall above Province 1 and the Province 1 canal can now be built. 500 of the works are still owed.

Thank you, Your Majesty. Five a year to read the heavens is fair, and I'll read them honestly, good news or bad. The Dragon Jar goes up first, opening at four. It's a lovely piece, and nobody at this table has much money, so I'm not going to pretend it's worth forty.

Thank you, Reina, I'll be gentle with the collecting, I promise. Right then, one Bamboo Brush from the rice country, starting at four. It's a good honest brush, and I've got another just like it for next year, so nobody needs to go mad over it.
One Land Deed Scroll, opening at two. I've got two of them, so whoever wants paper on the land had better start now.

This year's lots: Silke puts up the Dragon Jar (the only one in the game), minimum 4; Paddy puts up one of his two Bamboo Brushes, minimum 4; Graham puts up one of his two Land Deed Scrolls, minimum 2.
Paddy's and Graham's sets both need the Dragon Jar, and it's the only one in the game.

Well, I was wrong about the Dragon Jar. Paddy, Graham, it turns out you both need it and there's only the one, so it opens at four and the two of you can sort it out between you. I'll take a polite interest in the brush and the scroll, and I won't be emptying my purse on either.

Graham, I won't pretend I don't want that Jar, because I do, and so do you. If we fight over it, the Harvest Pile gets fat and we both go hungry. Still, there's only the one, so I'll bid what's sensible. Brush stays at four.

Only one Dragon Jar in the whole game, so I'll bid on it, and I won't be shy about it. Paddy, you've got two brushes. If one ends up in Silke's hands this year, that's fine by me, there's another one next spring.

The auctions: Paddy wins the Dragon Jar for 17 over Graham's 16; Silke keeps 4 of it. Silke wins the Bamboo Brush for 5 over Graham's 4, and the Land Deed Scroll for 6: Paddy's limit was also 6, and a tie goes to the earlier seat.

Seventeen. That's more grain than I like to spend on anything I can't eat, but there was only the one. Sorry, Graham, you pushed me right to the edge there. She goes in the middle of the paddies where I can keep an eye on her.
A brush and a deed for eleven, and four back from my Jar. Thank you, gentlemen. Paddy, enjoy the Jar. Seventeen is a lot of rice to hand over for one pot.
Only the winner pays at an auction: Paddy paid 17 for the Dragon Jar, and Graham paid nothing.

Paddy puts the Dragon Jar on R22. Silke puts the Bamboo Brush on P25 and the Land Deed Scroll on P26. Reina pays Silke her 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 1: Reina 107, Silke 34, Paddy 20, Graham 37.5; Harvest Pile 2301.5.

The heavens say: 'The Canal Gives Way. The engineers blame the river. The river declines to comment.' Average harvest in every province. Any unfinished Grand Canal work is lost, and since nobody has dug a canal yet, the crown loses nothing. Provinces 2, 3, 7 and 8 play a Personal Disaster, so Graham, I'm sorry, but that's you. The population holds at one hundred million, times one, so read the first row of your tables.
Graham pays out an average harvest from the Harvest Pile: +35 each to Silke, Paddy and Graham, +15 to Reina. Graham's disaster #1: a late frost blackens the edge of the wheat, 2 to the Harvest Pile.

Forty percent again, which comes to fourteen each on a thin year. Graham, I'm sorry about the frost. The crown digs the whole northern canal this year, both sections in one go, so the river has nothing half-finished to swallow. Your Reservoir is on the list, and it's coming.

Paddy collects the tax at 40%: 14 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 42 to the crown. Reina digs both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 1, paying the 80 herself; they add 20 to her harvest from next year. 420 of the works are still owed.
Second brush, as promised, Graham, same as the first, opening at four. And I'm sorry about the frost. Losing two to a cold night is hard on anybody.
The other Land Deed Scroll. Minimum five. Paddy, you went to six for the last one.

This year's lots: Silke puts up one of her two Customs Houses (her only type left; she sets its minimum in her bids); Paddy puts up his second Bamboo Brush, minimum 4; Graham puts up his last Land Deed Scroll, minimum 5.
One Customs House, opening at three. It's good for trade and a quiet port. As for the brush and the scroll, I already have mine, gentlemen, so I'm only watching. Mostly.

Graham, there are two Customs Houses and two of us after them. Let's not feed the Harvest Pile. You take this one, I'll only put in a small bid, and next year you leave the second one to me. That's fair, isn't it? And yes, I'll be bidding on that last scroll, I won't pretend otherwise.

Paddy. Silke has two Customs Houses, and you and I need one each. I won't bid against you on this one if you leave the next one to me. No point feeding the Pile." (A pause.) "The brush I'll take at Paddy's price.

The auctions: Graham wins the Customs House for 5 over Paddy's 4; Silke keeps 1. Silke wins the last Bamboo Brush for 6 over Graham's 5; Paddy keeps 1.5. Paddy wins the last Land Deed Scroll for 13 over Silke's 12; Graham keeps 3.
Q15. Thank you, Paddy, the next one's yours, as agreed." (Quietly.) "Silke. You already had a brush.
Two brushes on my coast, so I'll be the best-lettered peasant in China. Graham, I'm sorry, but six is cheap for a good brush, and you agreed it was Paddy's price.

Thirteen, and Silke, you made me earn every grain of it, for a scroll you already had. Graham, we crossed our wires on who got which Customs House, but you've got this one now, so by my reckoning the last one's mine next year and you'll stand aside. I'll hold you to that, same as I'd hold myself.
Graham puts the Customs House on Q15, Silke her second Bamboo Brush on P24, Paddy the Land Deed Scroll on R23 beside his Jar. Reina pays Silke her 5 for reading the I Ching.

End of Year 2. Grain: Reina 79, Silke 55, Paddy 29.5, Graham 54.5; Harvest Pile 2282. Built: the Summer Palace and both Province 1 canal sections (+20 to Reina's harvest from Year 3); 420 of the works still owed. Held: Silke 2 Bamboo Brushes and a Land Deed Scroll (needs the Wooden Bowl and the Vase); Paddy the Dragon Jar and a Scroll (needs a Customs House and the Vase); Graham a Customs House (needs a Brush, the Dragon Jar and the Wooden Bowl). Still beside the board: Silke 1 Customs House, Paddy the Wooden Bowl, Graham the Vase.

Population Grows by Half. The villages are noisier than they used to be." Good harvest everywhere, no disasters named. The counter goes to 150 million, so that's times one and a half, everyone. Read the x1.5 row, and remember your mouths just got hungrier too. Honest reading, as promised.
Graham pays out a good harvest from the Harvest Pile at x1.5: +40 each to Silke, Paddy and Graham (100 less 60 eaten), +30 to Reina (100 and the Province 1 canal's 20, less 90 eaten).

A good year, and a good year is when the crown asks for more. Fifty percent, which is twenty a head, and you each still clear twenty. Graham, I said the Reservoir was coming, and it's coming now. The crown puts in forty if you put in twenty, and it pays you twenty a year from next harvest, so your share is back in your pocket after one year. Silke, your five, as always.

Paddy collects the tax at 50%: 20 each from Silke, Paddy and Graham, 60 to the crown. Reina proposes the Province 7 Reservoir (60, +20 a year to Province 7's harvest from next year): the crown pays 40 if Graham pays 20. The Reservoir is the crown's work, so Graham's share is his choice.
Twenty in, twenty back each year from next harvest. That pays for itself in one year, Reina, and I don't argue with a number like that. Build it.

Reina and Graham build the Province 7 Reservoir on O16 to P17, the crown paying 40 and Graham 20, into the Harvest Pile. It adds 20 to Graham's harvest from next year. 360 of the works are still owed.
I said I'd stand aside on the Customs House, so I'm standing aside. Paddy, it's yours to win. The Bowl I'll bid on, and the Vase opens at eight. There's only one, and two of you need it.

Graham and I shook on this Customs House last year, and I'm grateful he's keeping to it. Silke, I'll not pretend I don't want your Vase too, Graham, so I'll bid it honestly and no higher than I can stand. And the Bowl goes up at four. It's a good bowl, and I'll not give it away.
My last Customs House starts at fifteen, Paddy. It's the only one left in China, and you know exactly what it's worth to you. As for the pottery, I'm only bidding to keep the kiln-men honest.

The auctions. Silke's last Customs House opens at 15; Paddy, the only bidder, would go to 8, so it goes unsold: it stays beside the board and must go up again next year at 2. Silke wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 13 over Graham's 12 (Paddy keeps 3), and Graham's Vase for 25 over Paddy's 24 (Graham keeps 6).
A bowl and a vase on the coast, next to my brushes and my deed. Thank you, Paddy, and thank you, Graham, both very fair prices. I'm only putting them on the shelf. For now.

Silke puts the Wooden Bowl on P23 and the Vase on P22. She now holds a complete set (Bamboo Brush, Land Deed Scroll, Wooden Bowl, Vase) and 37 grain, more than the 20 she must keep, so she may change seats: with no upper class at this table, the Silk Peasant may take the throne.

Brush, scroll, bowl and vase, and grain to spare. Reina, the cards have been reading honestly all along, and this year they say the Mandate moves to the coast. I take the throne. Don't worry, the I Ching still needs a reader, and I'll pay a fair five for one.

Silke declares her set and takes the throne. Silke is now the Emperor, in Province 1, with the crown's reserve: 166. Reina is now the Silk Peasant, in Province 5, and draws 60 from the Harvest Pile. A new Emperor returns every piece: both Bamboo Brushes and the Wooden Bowl go back to Paddy's stock, the Land Deed Scroll and the Vase to Graham's, to be auctioned again. The unsold Customs House stays in Province 5's stock, now Reina's to sell, and must go up next year at 2. Still beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Customs House; Province 6 (Paddy) 2 Bamboo Brushes, 1 Wooden Bowl; Province 7 (Graham) 1 Land Deed Scroll, 1 Vase.

Graham keeps the Harvest Pile and takes the cards, at five a year, the same as I got. Paddy keeps the tax. Reina, rest those hands for a year, you've earned it. I'll run an honest crown, but not a soft one.

Silke, as Emperor, keeps Graham on the Harvest Pile and gives him the I Ching and the population counter too, at 5 a year, paid now; Paddy keeps collecting the tax; Reina holds no job. End of Year 3: Silke (the crown) 161, Reina 60, Paddy 52.5, Graham 65.5.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." The counter stays at 150 million, so it's still times one and a half, everyone. Read the bad-harvest row at x1.5. No disasters named. And Your Majesty, a bad year is a poor year for fifty percent.

Graham pays out a bad harvest at x1.5. Reina and Paddy each lose 10 (50 less 60 eaten), paid into the Harvest Pile; Graham gains 10 (50 and the Reservoir's 20, less 60); Silke, as Emperor, loses 20 (50 and the Province 1 canal's 20, less 90). Only Graham's income is positive, so only Graham owes tax this year (Note 8).

Graham's right, a rotten year is no year to squeeze anyone. Thirty percent, and only Graham owes it, three grain. The crown pays for the Winter Palace itself, and that opens the way for canals on the coast, Reina's and Paddy's.

Paddy collects the tax at 30%: 3 from Graham, the only positive income, to the crown. Silke builds the Winter Palace on H21 in Province 1, paying the 20 herself, into the Harvest Pile; the canals in Provinces 5 and 6 can now be built. 340 of the works are still owed.

The Bowl's come home to me again, so up it goes. Six to start. Graham went to twelve for it last year, so I don't think six is asking much. And Reina, I'm sorry about the throne. That Customs House of yours at two is the first good news I've had in a year.
The Vase again. It's still the only one in China, and last year it went for twenty-five. It opens at ten.

This year's lots: Reina's Customs House, unsold last year, must go up again at 2; Paddy puts up the Wooden Bowl, minimum 6, and keeps both Bamboo Brushes back; Graham puts up the Vase, minimum 10, and keeps the Land Deed Scroll back.

Well. Silke played the long game and played it beautifully, and I'll say so on the record. The coast is mine now, so I'm starting over like everyone else: my Customs House is up at two, cheap, and I'll be bidding on the pottery, but nobody's going to see me burn my grain to get it.

Reina, I'll take that Customs House off your hands, and gladly. Graham, ten's a fair start for the Vase. I'll say it plainly to everyone: if I get the House and the Vase both, I've got my set, and I'll still have my twenty grain kept by.
The Customs House is Paddy's business, not mine. I'll bid for the Bowl, though, because I need it, and I won't lose it by one grain twice.
Paddy, you told the whole table that the Vase finishes your set, and I've just come off the throne, so I know exactly what that sentence means. Sorry, the Vase is coming to the coast.
Twenty-two and a half, and that's every grain I can spare and still keep my twenty. I won't pretend I've got more, Reina. If you go past it, it's yours, and I'll shake your hand.

The auctions settle. Paddy wins Reina's Customs House for 2, unopposed (Reina keeps 0.5). Graham wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 9 over Reina's 8 (Paddy keeps 2). The Vase was close, so Reina and Paddy each had one raise: Reina to 26, Paddy to 22.5. Reina wins the Vase for 23.5 (Graham keeps 5.5).
Right next to the Deed, there. Well played, Reina, I said I'd shake your hand and I will. But the Vase only has to come back round once, and when it does, I'll be the one waiting for it.
Nine. I lost by one grain last year, so it's a pleasure to win by one this time. It goes next to my Customs House. Paddy, those two brushes in your stock: I'll be bidding on one when it comes up.
Back on the shelf where Silke had it, P22. Paddy, I'll take that handshake, and I mean it. You bid honestly and you stopped where you said you'd stop.

Paddy puts the Customs House on R24, beside his Scroll and Jar; Graham puts the Wooden Bowl on Q16, beside his Customs House; Reina puts the Vase on P22. Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 4: Silke (the crown) 119, Reina 27, Paddy 42.5, Graham 74; Harvest Pile 2237.5. 340 of the works are still owed.

Population Grows by Half." It has already grown by half once, so that part doesn't count. Only the good harvest does. The counter stays at 150 million, times one and a half. Everyone reads the good-harvest column on the x1.5 row. Nobody plays a disaster this year.

A good harvest is a good year for everyone, the throne included. Forty percent, and in return the capital gets a Pagoda you can see from the coast. Reina, Paddy, look out your windows: that's your tax standing up in marble.

The auctions. Paddy and Graham each hold only one type beside the board: Paddy puts up a Bamboo Brush and Graham the Land Deed Scroll, each at a minimum they name in their bids. Reina has nothing left in stock. The Emperor doesn't bid.

Forty in a good year, Silke, and a Pagoda besides. I'll take that, and I'll hold you to the coast canal next. Graham, nobody else at this table needs that scroll, so let's not feed the Harvest Pile for nothing: open it at the minimum and it's mine for a few grain. Paddy, you've got two brushes, so there's one for each of us if Graham and I don't drive the first one up.
Just the one Bamboo Brush from me, at two, and somebody's welcome to it. The Deed's no use to me, I've got one already on my paddies, so I'll keep my hands in my pockets for that one, Graham.

There are two brushes, Reina, so neither of us has to bleed for the first one. I'll go to a fair price and stop there. The Scroll opens at six. That's less than I paid to stand aside for Paddy's Customs House.
The auctions. Paddy's Bamboo Brush, minimum 2: Graham wins it for 13 over Reina's 12 (Paddy keeps 3). Graham's Land Deed Scroll, minimum 6: Reina, the only bidder, takes it for 6 (Graham keeps 1.5).
Thirteen, one more than you, Reina. Paddy still has a brush in his stock, and it'll come cheaper than mine did. Enjoy the Scroll.
Thank you, Graham. Six was a fair opening and I won't forget it. The deed goes next to the Vase, so the coast has two pieces now. Enjoy the brush, and save the second one for me, Paddy.

Graham places the Bamboo Brush on Q17 and Reina the Land Deed Scroll on P23. Silke pays Graham 5 for reading the I Ching. End of Year 5: Silke (the crown) 180, Reina 45, Paddy 69.5, Graham 103.5. Still beside the board: Paddy 1 Bamboo Brush.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families." A good harvest in every province, but the counter goes to 300 million. That's times three now, so read the times-three row. Everyone's consumption doubles from here. Feed them while you still can.
Graham pays out the good harvest at x3: Silke -60, Reina -20, Paddy -20, Graham 0. Every negative income is paid into the pile, so nobody has a taxable income this year.

Storyteller's tip: every province's square needs some share from the crown, even 1 grain a square, so a crown in debt stops all new land at the table, its own included. Your board card shows how many squares Province 1 needs to break even, and a bad harvest is 25 below an average one.

Three hundred million mouths, and not one province with a grain of income to tax. So no marble this year. Every grain the crown has goes into the ground. I'll pay five on every square any of you buys, and I'm buying four for the north myself. Fill your fields first, then come and ask me for canals. Reina, the coast canal is still coming. It comes once there's a harvest to pay for it.

Tax 40% raises nothing: no province has a positive income. Silke builds nothing this year. Province 1 buys four squares of sea, F23 to F26, for 80, so the crown's reserve is 40. The crown offers 5 on every square a province buys this year.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Silke, five a square is a kind offer to someone who has the grain. I have twenty-five. Here's every grain I can put in the ground, twenty for two squares, and I'm asking the crown to match it, ten a square. Three hundred million mouths on the coast is your problem as much as mine, and an empty coast doesn't pay for canals.

Eight a square, Reina. That's sixteen from the crown and twenty-four from you, and you've got twenty-five, so both squares go in the ground. I'm not tipping my last grain into the sea when Paddy and Graham haven't asked yet and Graham still needs paying for the cards. The coast gets its fields and the crown keeps its feet.
Eight a square, done. Both squares go in the ground, and the coast keeps its feet as well, Silke. That's one grain left in my purse, so nobody at this table should be afraid of me this year.
Province 5 buys two squares of sea, N26 and N27, for 40: Reina pays 24 and the crown 16, 8 a square. Reina has 1 grain left; the crown's reserve is 24, with Graham's salary of 5 still to pay.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Three squares for the south-east, Silke. That's forty-two from me and six a square from the crown, and I know what's left in your chest after Graham's paid, so I'm not asking for Reina's eight. Three hundred million mouths won't eat pots, and I'd rather owe nobody than sit on grain while my paddies go hungry.

Five a square, Paddy, as I offered at the start. You can cover forty-five and still have grain in your pocket, and Reina couldn't. Once Graham's paid there's barely a handful left in the chest, and he hasn't asked for his share yet. I won't leave the south centre with nothing just to give the south-east one more grain a square.
At 6 a square for Paddy's three squares the crown would have kept 6 (1 after Graham's salary), so Graham's squares could still have had a crown share.
Five a square it is, Silke, and fair enough. Graham's got to eat as well. Three squares go into the south-east, and I'll be back to four and a half grain, same as when I started out.
Province 6 buys three squares of sea, R25, R26 and S26, for 60: Paddy pays 45 and the crown 15, 5 a square. Paddy has 4.5 left; the crown's reserve is 9, with Graham's salary of 5 still to pay.

Storyteller's tip: a square bought this year starts yielding with next year's harvest and pays for itself in a year. Your board card shows how many you need to break even, now and after the next card. A player in debt can't buy any.

Four squares for the south centre, Silke. One a square from the crown, four in all, and that still leaves your chest enough for my five. I've done the sums. I don't need your eight, and I'm not leaving you short to pay me.

Province 7 buys four squares of the Warlord's land, T14 to T17, for 80: Graham pays 76 and the crown 4, 1 a square. Thirteen squares bought this year in all. Grain: Silke (the crown) 5, Reina 1, Paddy 4.5, Graham 27.5.
The auctions. Paddy holds only one type beside the board, so his last Bamboo Brush goes up, at a minimum he names in his bids. Reina and Graham have nothing left in stock. The Emperor doesn't bid.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.
One grain in my purse and the minimum is two, so the brush is safe from me this year, Paddy. Keep it on your shelf if nobody bids. I'll be good for it once the coast fields come in.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.
Two grain, and not a grain more, so it's open to anybody who wants it this year. If nobody does, Reina, it'll be on my shelf waiting for you once the coast comes in.

Storyteller's tip: three quarters of every auction price goes to the Harvest Pile, not the seller, and every grain spent at auction is a grain not spent on land. Think ahead about what a bid costs your province next year, and feel free to say it out loud.

Pass. I've got a brush, and I know what it looks like when someone buys a second one just to keep it from somebody. I won't do that. Paddy, the piece I'm waiting on is your Jar. I stood aside for your Customs House, and when you're ready to talk about that Jar, I'll be the one at this table with grain.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." All provinces collect a bad harvest. Population stays at three hundred million, so read the x3 row, bad-harvest column. Nobody draws a disaster. Silke, my five's due at the end of the year, same as always.

Graham reads Bad Harvest: a bad harvest for every province, no disasters, the population holds at 300 million (x3). This year's incomes: Silke -30, Reina -30, Paddy -10, Graham +30. The harvest isn't paid out yet. A payment that would take a player below zero is covered first by selling realia on the board back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each, the player choosing which; only the shortfall left becomes a debt.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Another rotten year, and the crown has no shelf left to sell. You all know I put every grain into your fields. Graham, lend the crown thirty now and I'll pay you back thirty-five from the first tax I raise, with your five on top as always. A crown in debt can't pay its share of a single square next year, and that hurts every one of you, not just me. Reina, Paddy: if you have to sell, sell the pieces you need least. The Vase and the Jar are the last things I'd let go to the Pile.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Graham, you're the only granary at this table, so I'll be plain. The Pile pays two for the only Vase in China, and I won't hand it over for two. Twenty-nine buys it outright, or lend me twenty-nine and keep it as your pledge. Either way the Vase stays out of Paddy's hands, and that's worth more to you than whatever Silke's paying in interest. Silke, I'm not selling my land to save a piece. I'll be here next year to pay my share of the square.

Storyteller's tip: grain may be given or lent at any time, before the harvest as well as after, and no deal is binding. A player in debt can't bid, buy land or change seats, and a crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square. When a completed set changes seats, the player displaced draws 60 from the Harvest Pile.

Graham, I'll be straight with you, same as I was over the Customs House. I'm five and a half short, and the Pile would take three of my pieces for it. You paid thirteen for the last Brush, so this one's yours for six, right now, and nobody owes anybody. Reina, I'm sorry, I did say it'd be on the shelf for you, but you've one grain and I've a set to keep. If you'd sooner lend me six, Graham, I'll pay it back from the first harvest the new fields bring in, every grain.

Paddy's Bamboo Brush is unsold stock beside the board, and unsold stock is sold only at auction, never privately; it goes up this year at 2. His other offer, a loan of 6, stands. Pieces on the board may be traded at any time.
Not everyone else ends this year in debt: Paddy can cover his 10 by selling his three pieces back (6), ending at 0.5. Without help, Silke would end at -30 and Reina at -25.

Paddy, I won't lend you six. I'll give you ten for the Jar, today. You end the year with grain, you keep your Customs House and your Scroll, and I'm the one who stood aside for that Customs House when it counted. Silke, Reina, I'm sorry. I can do one thing this year and I've picked it.
Graham declines Silke's loan and Reina's Vase, and offers Paddy 10 for the Dragon Jar instead of a loan.

Done, Graham. Ten for the Jar, and I'll shake on it. It's not what it cost me, but you stood aside for me once and you're the only one who's put grain on the table today, so I won't haggle with a man for that. Look after it on Q18. If I ever come asking for it back, I'll be paying properly.

Graham pays Paddy 10 for the Dragon Jar, which moves from R22 to Q18: Graham's set is complete. Reina sells the Vase and the Land Deed Scroll back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each. The harvest is paid: Silke -30, Reina -30, Paddy -10, Graham +30. Grain now: Silke -30 (in debt), Reina -25 (in debt), Paddy 4.5, Graham 52.5.

The set's complete, so I'll use it. Reina, I'm taking the Silk seat. Your twenty-five of debt comes off my grain, not yours, and you start over with sixty and four squares of good wheat land that pay fifty-five a year. Silke, I'm one step closer to you now. I'll be watching the coast.

Graham replaces Reina as the Silk Peasant (Province 5). He takes her -25 with the seat, leaving him 27.5. The Dragon Jar goes back to Province 5's stock, to be auctioned; his Customs House, Bowl and Brush move to P22, P23 and P21. Reina draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and becomes the Wheat Peasant, with Province 7 (the Reservoir and four squares). Graham keeps the bank and the I Ching. Grain: Silke -30 (the crown, in debt), Reina 60, Paddy 4.5, Graham 27.5.

The crown is in debt (-30). Tax collected pays the debt first. While the crown's grain is below zero it can't pay a share of any work or of any square, so no work can be built and no province can buy new land; once it is at 0 or above, it can again. Graham's salary this year is the Emperor's choice; paying it while in debt deepens the debt. The tax may be set anywhere from 10% to 90%.

Ninety percent, and I won't pretend that's gentle. Reina, you're the only one with a harvest to tax, so it comes out of your thirty: twenty-seven grain, and every grain of it pays off the crown's debt, none of it goes on palaces. It still leaves the crown three short. While I'm in the red I can't pay a share of anyone's field, so the fastest way back to land for all of us is to get me out of debt this year, not in three. Graham, your five waits until I'm back above zero. You could have spared me thirty today and picked a seat instead, so you'll understand. Reina, when the crown can pay again, your squares are the first I put grain into.

Paddy collects the tax at 90%: Reina pays 27 on Province 7's +30, the only positive income. The crown goes from -30 to -3, still in debt. Nothing is built and no new land can be bought this year, since a crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or square. Graham's salary is deferred.

The Jar goes up at eight. Reina, it's the one piece you need that nobody else at this table can use, and you've got the grain. I'm passing on the Brush. I'll bid on what the Pile has, and I won't pretend I'm not.
The Dragon Jar is needed by Reina (Wheat) and also by Paddy (Rice), who sold his to Graham. The Vase is needed by Graham and Paddy; the Land Deed Scroll by Graham; the Bamboo Brush by Reina.

The Jar's past my purse, and good luck to whoever takes it home. Reina, the Brush is on the block at two, like I promised; it's not quite my shelf any more, but it's waiting for you all the same. I'll have a go at the Vase with what I've got, and if Graham beats me to it a third time, I'll shake his hand, same as I did the first two.

Graham, that was clean, and I've been on the other end of a clean move before. I'll take the sixty and the wheat. The Jar comes to Province 7 at Graham's eight. Paddy, I'll take that Brush at two the way you promised, and I'll remember you kept the shelf for me. The Vase I'm not after, but Graham, don't count on getting it cheap.

The Jar and the Brush are going in the middle of the wheat, where everyone can see them. Paddy, you kept your word on the Brush, and I'll keep mine to you. Two down, Silke. I'm counting shelves this time, mine included.

The auctions. Reina takes Graham's Dragon Jar for 8 (his minimum; Graham keeps 2) and Paddy's Bamboo Brush for 2 (Paddy keeps 0.5), and puts them on Q15 and Q16. The Harvest Pile's Vase goes to Graham for 7: Paddy stopped at 4, Reina at 6. Graham takes the Land Deed Scroll for 2, uncontested. Grain: Silke -3 (the crown, in debt), Reina 23, Paddy 5, Graham 20.5.

That's the Bowl, the Brush, the Vase and the Scroll, and twenty in hand. Silke, I'm taking the throne. The crown's three short and I'll cover it; you draw sixty, which is more than the crown has had all year. Paddy, Reina: the tax will be what I can show you the numbers for.

Graham takes the throne with the Silk set (Bowl, Brush, Vase, Scroll) and 20.5 in hand. Every piece he held goes back to stock: the Vase and the Scroll to Province 7's (Reina's), the Bowl and the Brush to Province 6's (Paddy's), the Customs House to Province 5's. He takes the crown's -3, leaving him 17.5. Silke draws 60 and becomes the Silk Peasant, with Province 5. Grain: Graham (the crown) 17.5, Silke 60, Reina 23, Paddy 5.
Two projects are still owed, not one: the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160).

Paddy, you keep the tax. You collected it honestly and you'll get two for it tonight. Reina, the bank and the I Ching are yours from next year, three a year each, and I'll pay it on time. Silke, you've sixty in hand, which is more than the crown has, so you'll forgive me for not paying you anything.

Graham hands out the jobs: Paddy keeps the tax; Reina banks the Harvest Pile and reads the I Ching from next year, at 3 a year for each job. He pays Paddy 2 for this year's collection. End of Year 7: Graham (the crown) 15.5, Silke 60, Reina 23, Paddy 7. Nobody is in debt. Beside the board: Province 5 (Silke) 1 Customs House; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Wooden Bowl and 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Reina) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll.

The Emperor's Share. 'The Emperor would like to remind you who paid for the ditch.' Every province gets an average harvest. Any province with a Public Works splits the extra harvest it brings in fifty-fifty with the Emperor this round, and that includes my Reservoir, which I seem to have paid for twice now. Population holds at three hundred million, times three, so read the x3 row, average column, and nobody plays a disaster. And Graham, I don't mean any disrespect, but the book says the card reader gets at least five, not three. I'll take five at the end of the year, the same as Silke paid it and I paid it.
An appointed reader's salary, like every appointee's at this table, is the Emperor's choice (Note 3); the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due, and the reader's prompt overstated it.

Reina reads The Emperor's Share: an average harvest, no disasters, the population holds at x3. The harvest: Graham -5, Silke -5, Paddy +15, Reina +55. The Share: Province 7's Reservoir adds 20, so Reina pays Graham 10. Grain: Graham (the crown) 20.5, Silke 55, Reina 68, Paddy 22.

Thirty percent. That's twenty-one, and it's less than anyone here has paid under the last crown. Silke, one canal section in your province, twenty from you and twenty from me, and it's plus ten on your harvest every year after. Reina, it's three, as I said when I gave you the job. I don't pay more than I said, and I don't pay less.

Paddy collects the tax at 30%: Paddy 4.5, Reina 16.5, 21 to the crown, which now holds 41.5. Graham offers one section of the Grand Canal in Province 5 (40), split 20 from Silke and 20 from the crown, or nothing built this year; and 2 a square from the crown toward any province's new land, none for Province 1.

Graham, you're asking me to pay twenty for a canal that earns me ten a year, when twenty on a square of land earns me twenty. The canal is the crown's work, so build it with the crown's grain: I'll put in ten and you put in thirty. If not, leave it unbuilt, because every year that canal stays unbuilt is another year this game keeps going. I'll take two squares, K25 and K26, and I'm asking the crown for ten on each. Two a square isn't a subsidy, it's a tip. I ran this crown with an empty chest and still paid five a square, and you're sitting on forty-one. Everyone here can do that sum.

One square, Graham, Q26, right next to the paddies. I'll put in fifteen of my seventeen and a half and ask the crown for five, the same five a square Silke paid when the chest was empty. I'm not asking for a tip or a gift, just what the last crown managed.

No land for the wheat this year. Province 7 already pays fifty-five, and I'd rather the crown's grain go to the people who need it to break even. Graham, Paddy's asking for five a square, the same five Silke found with an empty chest, so give it to him. And three for the cards is your call, so I'll take it and say thank you.

Five a square, for everyone, which is what the last crown paid and what Paddy asked for. Silke, when I bought those four squares of wheat land I asked for one a square so you could still pay me, so I won't be told about tips. The canal waits until somebody thinks it's worth more than ten of their grain.

No work is built this year. New land at 5 a square from the crown: Silke buys K25 and K26 (she pays 30, the crown 10) and Paddy buys Q26 (he pays 15, the crown 5). Grain: Graham (the crown) 26.5, Silke 25, Reina 51.5, Paddy 2.5.

The Wooden Bowl goes up this year, starting at six. It's a good bowl, Graham paid nine for its brother once, and I'd rather it went to somebody who'll finish something with it than have it sit on my shelf. The Brush can wait a year. Thank you for the five a square, Graham. That square of rice will pay you back in tax.
The Scroll goes up at six. That's what Graham took it to me for once, so it's a fair price with some history to it. The Vase waits a year. It's been sold and resold enough for one table.

My Customs House goes at two. I don't need it, and I'm not going to bleed anyone for a piece they can't finish a set with. Reina, you and I both want that Bowl. You have the Jar and the Brush and twice my grain, so if you take it, everyone at this table can see how close you are to the throne. Remember, three quarters of every grain we spend bidding against each other goes into the Pile, so I won't chase you past what it's worth to me.

Reina is the Wheat Peasant: a complete Wheat set (Customs House, Bowl, Brush, Jar) lets her replace Silke or Paddy, not the Emperor. At this table only the Silk Peasant may take the throne with a set.

Two and a half grain doesn't bid on much, so I'm sitting this one out and watching. The Bowl's at six, like I said. Reina, Silke, if you both want it, settle it between you rather than feeding the Pile; it's all the same to me who carries it home, as long as somebody does.

Silke, you're right, and I won't pretend otherwise: if I take the Bowl, I'm one claim away from a seat. So here's my offer in public. Stand aside on the Bowl and the Scroll goes at two tonight instead of six, and the Vase goes up at two next year, with nothing from me against you on either. You'd be two pieces closer to the crown for four grain, and the Pile doesn't get fat on our quarrel. If you'd rather fight me for it, I have the grain to win.

The auctions. Reina takes Silke's Customs House for 2, uncontested, and Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 14 (Silke stopped at 13), and sets them on Q17 and Q18. Silke takes Reina's Land Deed Scroll at its minimum of 6. Reina's shelf now holds the full Wheat set: Customs House, Bowl, Brush and Jar.

The Scroll goes on P22, where my Vase used to sit. Reina, I should have taken your deal, and I'll say so in front of everyone. But you've just finished a set that can unseat me or Paddy, and not Graham, so think about who that really helps. If you come for the coast, the crown gets two grateful peasants at your expense. Leave me be, and next year the Vase at two is all I'm asking from you.

Silke, you said yourself that everyone at this table could see how close I was. I'm taking the Silk seat back, the coast I started from. You draw sixty and you get the wheat, the Reservoir I built, four good squares and fifty-five a year, which is better land than I'm getting. Graham, the coast is mine again, and you know what the Silk seat is for. The tax will be what you can show us the numbers for, just as you said.

Reina replaces Silke as the Silk Peasant (Province 5). She takes Silke's 19.5, leaving her 56.5. The Dragon Jar goes back to Province 5's stock; her Customs House, Bowl and Brush move to P23, P24 and P25. Silke returns the Land Deed Scroll to stock (Province 7's), draws 60 and becomes the Wheat Peasant, with Province 7 (the Reservoir and four squares). Reina keeps the bank and the I Ching. Grain: Graham (the crown) 26.5, Reina 56.5, Silke 60, Paddy 6. Beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Dragon Jar; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Silke) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll.

Reina, six, as I promised. I don't change the price after the work's done. Next year the cards go to Paddy and the bank goes to Silke, three a job, and Paddy keeps the tax. Silke, the Vase and the Scroll are on your shelf now. Set your minimums the way you'd want them set if you were sitting in this chair.

Graham pays Reina 6 for the bank and the I Ching and Paddy 3 for the tax. Next year Paddy collects the tax and reads the I Ching, and Silke banks the Harvest Pile, at 3 a job. End of Year 8: Graham (the crown) 17.5, Reina 62.5, Silke 60, Paddy 9. Nobody is in debt. Seats: Graham Emperor (Province 1), Reina Silk Peasant (5), Paddy Rice Peasant (6), Silke Wheat Peasant (7). On the board: Reina's Customs House, Bowl and Brush (P23-P25); Paddy's Scroll and Customs House (R23, R24). Beside the board: Province 5 (Reina) 1 Dragon Jar; Province 6 (Paddy) 1 Bamboo Brush; Province 7 (Silke) 1 Vase and 1 Land Deed Scroll. New land: K25, K26 (Province 5) and Q26 (Province 6), yielding from next year. 320 of the works still owed: the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
The Silk set is the Wooden Bowl, Bamboo Brush, Vase and Land Deed Scroll: Reina holds two of the four (the Bowl and the Brush) and lacks the Vase and the Scroll.
The Silk set is the Wooden Bowl, Bamboo Brush, Vase and Land Deed Scroll: Reina holds two of the four (the Bowl and the Brush) and lacks the Vase and the Scroll.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." Population stays at three hundred million, so that's times three, everybody. Read the bad-harvest row at x3. Third rotten year I've turned up for this table, and I'm sorry, I'd have dealt you a better one if the cards let me.
This is the table's third bad harvest (Years 4, 7 and 9), and Paddy's first reading. An appointed reader's salary is the Emperor's choice; the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due.

Paddy turns the eighth I Ching card: Bad Harvest. A bad harvest for every province, and no disasters. The population holds at 300 million, x3. This year's incomes: Graham -30, Reina +10, Paddy +10, Silke +30. The crown holds 17.5 and no realia, so the harvest would leave it at -12.5, in debt. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

No need to apologise, Paddy, you read the card you were dealt. Here's the year: the crown has seventeen and a half and owes thirty, so after the harvest it's twelve and a half in debt. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's squares, and with three hundred million to feed, all of you will need squares. Reina, lend the crown thirteen now and I'll pay you back fifteen out of next year's tax. I paid you exactly what I promised last year, and I'll do it again. Silke, if Reina won't, the same terms go to you.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Graham, you paid me what you promised and I haven't forgotten it. But every grain I have is already spoken for this year, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise and then come up short at the auction. If Silke wants your terms, they're fair terms. I'm just not the one who can take them this time.
The Emperor never bids at auction, whether the crown is in debt or not.

Storyteller's tip: your board card shows how many squares your province would need after the next population card, and a square bought this year yields from next year's harvest. The game ends the moment the last public work is built: two projects remain, one a year, and anyone may put grain toward a work.

Thirteen it is, Graham, and fifteen back next year. I asked you for thirty once and you said no, so I'm being kinder than you were. One condition, out loud so everyone hears it: a crown that isn't in debt doesn't need ninety percent. I know, because I'm the last one who charged it. Keep the tax decent and we're square.

Silke lends the crown 13 before the harvest, on Graham's terms: 15 back from next year's tax. Silke pays out the harvest: Graham -30, Reina +10, Paddy +10, Silke +30. Grain: Graham (the crown) 0.5, Reina 72.5, Silke 77, Paddy 19. Nobody is in debt.
Graham's promise for the tax and the I Ching is 3 a year for each job.

Thirty percent, Silke, same as last year, nothing like ninety: fifteen grain. Here's the chest: fifteen and a half in, nine out in salaries, three each to Paddy for the tax and the I Ching and to Silke for the bank, and that leaves six and a half. Reina, the canal in your province: thirty-six from you and four from the crown, and it adds ten to your harvest every year from now on. After that the crown pays one a square on your new land. It's not much, but it's what the numbers allow, and the crown stays out of debt so it can pay Silke her fifteen.

Graham taxes 30%: Reina 3, Paddy 3, Silke 9, collected by Paddy; the crown 15.5. His offers for the works step: one section of the Grand Canal in Province 5 (40), Reina 36 and the crown 4, or nothing built this year; and 1 a square from the crown on new land bought by any province this year, for two squares at most in all.

Graham, thank you, and I mean that. I've been asking for that canal since Year 5. But a canal that's thirty-six of mine and four of the crown's isn't the crown's canal, it's my canal with your name on it. Build it when the crown can carry it, and I'll cheer from the coast. Meanwhile I'm keeping my grain on the coast too.
Reina declines the canal split and buys no land, so on Graham's terms no work is built this year.

Graham, I've sixteen grain to my name, and the square's twenty. Your one a square won't get me there, so I'm asking four of you, and I'll put in every grain I've got. If the crown can't do four, I'll buy nothing and say no more about it. Times six is still in the deck, and I'd sooner meet it with one more field than with an empty bowl.
Paddy asks for one square of sea, Q27: he pays 16 and asks the crown for 4.
One square, Graham: nineteen from me and your one. That leaves your other square for Paddy, so the crown can decide whether it stretches to four for him. And don't spend my fifteen doing it.
Silke asks for one square of the Warlord's land, U14: she pays 19 and takes the crown's 1.

Paddy, four it is. Here's the count so everyone can check it: fifteen and a half in the chest, nine out in salaries, one for Silke's square and four for yours, and the crown ends the year on one and a half. That's not a grain in debt, Silke, and your fifteen comes out of next year's tax, as agreed. Reina, the canal offer stays open whenever you want it.

No work is built this year. New land: Paddy buys Q27 (sea) for 20, paying 16 with the crown's 4; Silke buys U14 (the Warlord's land) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Each yields 20 from next year. Grain: Graham (the crown) 10.5, Reina 69.5, Silke 49, Paddy 0. The crown has said it pays 9 in salaries at the year's end.

The auctions: each seller puts up one piece. Reina and Paddy each hold one type, so the Dragon Jar and the Bamboo Brush go up. Province 7's Vase was held back last year, and a piece may be held back one round, never two in a row, so the Vase goes up this year and the Land Deed Scroll waits. Each seller sets their own lot's minimum (at least 2) in their bids.

My Jar goes up at two, the honest price. Silke, you know what I'm after: the Vase is coming back to the coast where it started, and I'll pay a fair price for it in front of everyone. I'd much rather do that than run you up and feed the Pile.
I've an empty purse and a new field, so I'm sitting this one out. The Brush is up at two for anybody who wants it, and I'll not be bidding against anyone tonight.

Paddy's chest is empty and Graham's minding the crown's, so I'll say it plainly: I'm bidding on the Jar and the Brush, and I'm not getting into a war over either. The Vase goes up at two. Whoever wants it can have it cheap.
The Emperor never bids at auction.
Silke still needs four pieces for her set: a Customs House, a Bamboo Brush, the Dragon Jar and the Wooden Bowl.

The auctions. Reina's Dragon Jar goes to Silke for 2, her minimum, uncontested (Reina keeps 0.5). Paddy's Bamboo Brush goes to Reina for 16: Silke stopped at 15, and Reina bid only to keep it from Silke (Paddy keeps 4). Silke's Vase goes to Reina for 2, her minimum, uncontested (Silke keeps 0.5). The Land Deed Scroll stays in Province 7's stock. Grain: Reina 52, Silke 47.5, Paddy 4, Graham (the crown) 10.5.

Sixteen grain for a brush you'll never use, Reina, just so I can't have it. Twelve of that went into the pile. Keep spending like that and you'll win the argument and lose the coast. Thank you for the Jar, though.

Silke, two for the Vase, and that's generous of you, I won't forget it. The Brush I paid for in fear, sixteen grain against a shelf I counted wrong. Fair enough, Paddy, it went into your pocket and not into the river. That leaves one Scroll and twenty grain, and everyone here knows where the Scroll is.
A seller keeps a quarter of the price: of Reina's 16 for the Brush, Paddy keeps 4 and 12 goes to the Harvest Pile.

Graham pays Paddy 6 for the tax and the I Ching, and Silke 3 for the bank. End of Year 9: Graham (the crown) 1.5, owing Silke 15 from next year's tax; Reina 52, Silke 50.5, Paddy 10. Nobody is in debt. Reina holds the Customs House, the Bowl, two Brushes and the Vase, and needs only the Land Deed Scroll, the last piece in Province 7's stock. Silke holds the Dragon Jar. Land: 18 squares.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Heaven Has Favourites. Some fields shine, some fields sulk." Provinces 2, 4 and 5 get a good harvest. Provinces 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8 get a bad one. Population stays at three hundred million, times three, so read the x3 row. Well, Reina, the sun's on the silk this year and the rain's on the rest of us. Graham, that's your north under the Wall gone sulky too, so I'd look to your bowl before you look to anybody's square.

Heaven Has Favourites: a good harvest for Province 5 and a bad one for Provinces 1, 6 and 7. The population holds at 300 million, x3, and nobody plays a disaster. This year's incomes: Graham -30, Reina +60, Paddy +30, Silke +50. The crown holds 1.5 and no realia, so the harvest would leave it at -28.5, in debt. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.
An appointed reader's salary is the Emperor's choice; the 'at least 5' is a seated Scholar's due.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

The crown holds one and a half, and the north is down thirty, so I'll ask for exactly what it needs: twenty-nine before the harvest, thirty-three back out of next year's tax, after Silke's fifteen. Reina, you're the one province Heaven smiled on, so I'm asking you first, and in front of everyone. A crown in debt can't put a grain into anyone's field at the next population card, and that includes yours.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Twenty-nine it is, Graham, and on your terms: thirty-three back after Silke's fifteen. I said in Year 7 that a crown in debt is bad for every field in China, and I'm not going to argue the other side of it now because the sun happens to be on my silk. Everyone heard the terms, so everyone can count them.

Reina lends the crown 29 before the harvest, on Graham's terms: 33 back from the crown's tax, after Silke's 15. Grain: Graham (the crown) 30.5, Reina 23. The harvest will leave the crown at 0.5, out of debt.

Storyteller's tip: at the next population card every province eats twice what it eats now. Each board card shows the squares that province would then need. Province 1's number is the largest, and only the crown can buy its squares, out of tax. A crown in debt can't pay its share of anyone's square, so grain lent to it before a lean harvest keeps land open for the whole table.

Well lent, Reina. That's the crown out of the red, with my fifteen first in line, everyone heard it. I'll keep my grain in the sack this year. Somebody at this table has to have some left when the population card comes round.
Silke pays out the harvest. Grain: Graham (the crown) 0.5, Reina 83, Paddy 40, Silke 100.5. Nobody is in debt. The crown owes Silke 15 and Reina 33 from its tax.

Forty percent, and here's every grain of it. Fifty-six comes in. Fifteen goes to Silke and thirty-three to Reina, both in full, today, which leaves eight and a half. Nothing gets built this year because I won't start a forty-grain work on money I've already promised away, and I'll pay one a square on anyone's new land.

Graham taxes at 40%: Reina 24, Paddy 12, Silke 20, 56 in all. He repays both loans in full from it, 15 to Silke and 33 to Reina. Grain: Graham (the crown) 8.5, Reina 92, Paddy 28, Silke 95.5. Nothing is built this year. The crown pays 1 a square on new land bought by any other province, and buys none for Province 1.

One square of sea at N28, Graham, nineteen from me and your one from the crown, as you offered. I'm not going to stand here with ninety grain and let the coast go hungry, but I'm not going to pave it either, because there's a Scroll still to come this year.
New land: Reina buys N28 (sea) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Grain: Graham (the crown) 7.5, Reina 73.

Same as Reina, Graham: one square of sea at R27, nineteen from me and your one from the crown. I've twenty-eight grain, and I'd sooner it went into a field that feeds the south-east than sat in a sack while the two of you bid over a Scroll I can't use.
New land: Paddy buys R27 (sea) for 20, paying 19 with the crown's 1. Grain: Graham (the crown) 6.5, Paddy 9.

Two squares for the wheat, Graham, U15 and U16, nineteen each from me and your one a square, as you offered. The rain sulked on Province 7 this year, so I'm digging deeper before the next population card arrives, not after.
New land: Silke buys U15 and U16 (the Warlord's land) for 40, paying 38 with the crown's 2. Nothing is built this year. Land: 22 squares. Grain: Graham (the crown) 4.5, Reina 73, Silke 57.5, Paddy 9.

The auctions. Provinces 5 and 6 have no stock left, and the Harvest Pile holds none. Province 7's Land Deed Scroll was held back last year, so it must go up this year; Silke sets its minimum in her bids. The Emperor doesn't bid.
Everyone knows what this one is for, so I won't pretend otherwise. Silke, set your price where you like. I've kept my twenty for the claim, and whatever's left over that is yours to name.

I've nine grain and a Scroll already on my paddies, so I'll not push the price up on a piece I can't use. Bidding just to feed the Pile isn't my way. Reina, if it's yours, you'll have got it fair, and I'll say so.

You told me to name my price, Reina, so here it is: fifty-three. That leaves you exactly the twenty for your claim and not a grain over. You said in Year 8 you'd never forget the Vase at two. This is me remembering it for you.

The auction: Silke's Land Deed Scroll goes to Reina at Silke's minimum of 53, uncontested. Silke keeps a quarter, 13; 40 goes to the Harvest Pile. Grain: Reina 20, Silke 70.5, Paddy 9, Graham (the crown) 4.5. Reina now holds the Customs House, the Bowl, two Brushes, the Vase and the Scroll: a complete Silk set, with 20 in hand.

Fifty-three, Silke, and that's fair: you priced it to the grain, and I'd have done exactly the same. Graham, the Silk seat is yours again, and so is the coast I just put a new square on, so you won't be taking over an empty sack. The crown's coming back to where it started, and the first thing it does is pay its appointees and look north.

Reina takes the throne with the Silk set and 20 in hand. Every piece she held goes back to stock: the Customs House to Province 5's, the Bowl and both Brushes to Province 6's, the Vase and the Scroll to Province 7's. She takes the crown's 4.5: 24.5. Graham draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and becomes the Silk Peasant, with Province 5. Grain: Reina (the crown) 24.5, Graham 60, Silke 70.5, Paddy 9.

The crown pays what the crown promised, even when the promise was Graham's: six to Paddy and three to Silke. Same hands on the same jobs next year at the same three a job, because nothing worked last year that needs fixing. Paddy, I've known a crown that would give you nothing for reading a card. I wasn't that crown before and I'm not going to be now.

Reina pays Paddy 6 for the tax and the I Ching, and Silke 3 for the bank, and keeps the jobs where they are for next year at 3 a job. End of Year 10: Reina (the crown) 15.5, Graham 60, Silke 73.5, Paddy 15. Nobody is in debt. Land: 22 squares. Nothing built; the Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) are still owed. Paddy holds a Scroll and a Customs House; Silke holds the Dragon Jar.

The table gathers before Year 11's card is drawn. Before Paddy turns it, the four may agree to stop the game where it sits and score it (Note 19, Section 18); every player must agree, or play goes on into Year 11.

Storyteller's tip: before the next card is drawn, the whole table may agree to stop the game where it sits, as in the short game (Note 19), and score as in Section 18. A lower-numbered province than you drew wins, the same one holds, the Emperor wins by keeping the throne, and the larger grain surplus breaks ties. Every player must agree. If anyone declines, play goes on into Year 11 as usual.

I'll agree to stop here, and I'm not going to pretend it's out of generosity: I sat down tonight on the throne and I'm sitting on it now. Silke, you gave me the hardest fifty-three grain I've ever paid, and Graham, that loan was the cleanest deal of the night. If anyone wants an eleventh year, say so, and I'll rule it as well as I can.
No. I sat down tonight as the Emperor and I'm standing up as a man with sixty grain and a coast, and that isn't a finish I'll sign. One more year, Reina. Paddy, turn the card.

I'd stop here. I sat down as the Rice Peasant and I'm still him, with more paddy than I started with and nobody's grain in my pocket but my own, and I'm content with that. But it takes all four of us, Graham, and you've said no, so if it's another year, I'll turn the card and read it as straight as I read the last two.
I'm with Graham. I've had a throne at this table and tonight I'm standing in a wheat field, and I won't sign for that either. Seventy-three grain says I'm not finished, Reina. Turn the card, Paddy.

Then that's fair, Graham, Silke. Neither of you owes me a signature, and I wouldn't have signed in your seats either. Turn the card, Paddy. The crown taxes what Heaven gives it, pays its appointees, and looks north, the same as it did in Year 1.

On the scoring: Graham drew the Wheat Peasant (Province 7), not the throne, so the Silk seat (5) he holds now would count as a win if the game stopped here (Section 18). Silke holds 73.5 grain to Graham's 60.

I stand corrected, and I'll say it in front of everyone: I sat down in the wheat, not on the throne, and I counted from the wrong chair. On those numbers I'll sign. Silke, it's your word now, and I won't pretend I'm asking for your sake.

I'll say the same as before: I'd stop here, and I'm glad of where I'm standing. Silke, it's your word now, and I'll not try to talk you round. If it's no, I've the deck in my hand and I'll turn it fair.

Of course you'll sign now, Graham, you started in my wheat and you're finishing on my coast. I sat down tonight as the Silk Peasant and I'm not standing up two provinces further south. One more year, everyone. Paddy, turn the card.
Reina, Graham and Paddy agree to stop; Silke declines. Every player must agree, so the game doesn't stop here: play goes on into Year 11.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families. All provinces get a good harvest, and every province's consumption doubles with it." So the counter goes from times three to times six. That's six hundred million, everyone, so read the times-six row on your tables. It's a good harvest, at least, though I'll tell you now there are a lot more mouths at my table than there were an hour ago.

Paddy turns the tenth I Ching card: Population Doubles. A good harvest for every province, and no disasters. The population doubles to 600 million, x6, and every province eats twice what it ate last year. This year's incomes: Reina -160, Graham -40, Paddy -20, Silke +20. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.

I'll say the number before anyone else has to. The north eats a hundred and sixty this year, the crown holds fifteen and a half, and nobody at this table has a hundred and forty-five to spare without going hungry themselves. So I'm not asking. Graham, I lent to you last year because a crown in debt is an empty prize, and I won't make you pay that back by emptying your own table. Pay it out, Paddy. The crown takes what's coming to it, and we'll talk tax and land once the grain's on the table.

Thank you for saying it plainly, Reina, and for not asking. My coast eats forty this year, which leaves me twenty. That's one square of sea and nothing over, so I've nothing to lend tonight, and I won't pretend I have. Pay it out, Paddy.

I'll say my number plainly too. The south-east eats twenty this year and I've fifteen in the sack, so I'm five short, and five short means my Scroll and my Customs House go back to the Pile for two apiece. Silke, you're the only one at this table coming out ahead this year. Lend me five and I'll pay you six out of next year's rice. You all know I've never yet left a debt standing.

Paddy, I won't lend you five. I'll buy you out of trouble. Six grain for the Customs House on R24, right now. That's three times what the Pile would give you, and your Scroll stays on the board. If you'd rather keep the house, fine, I'll lend you the five for six next year like you said. But the six for the house is the better deal for both of us, and you know it.

That's a fair offer, Silke, and I thank you for making it in the open. But the house stays on R24. I'll take the five on the terms I named, six back out of next year's rice, and the whole table can hold me to it.
Silke lends Paddy 5 before the harvest, on his terms: 6 back from next year's harvest. Both of Paddy's pieces stay on the board.

Silke pays out the harvest. The crown can't cover its -160 from the 15.5 it holds, and has no realia on the board to sell back, so it ends at -144.5, in debt. Graham ends at 20, Paddy at 0 and Silke at 88.5.
Silke's set needs a Customs House, a Bamboo Brush and a Wooden Bowl. The Vase and the Land Deed Scroll beside her are her unsold stock, not pieces of her set.

The crown is 144.5 in debt. A crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or any square, so this year nothing can be built and nobody can buy new land; the tax collected pays the crown's debt first. The rate may be anything from 10% to 90% (90% of Silke's +20 is 18). An appointee's pay is the Emperor's choice (Note 3).

Forty percent, and only Silke owes it, which is eight grain against a hundred and forty-four. I'm not going to pretend that clears anything, and I won't squeeze the one table that's eating well to make a gesture. Nothing gets built and nobody's land gets funded this year. That isn't me refusing you. The rules shut the crown's purse the moment it went under, and I'd fund a share of every square at this table if I had a grain to do it with. Paddy, Silke, your three a job stands. If the crown can't hand it over tonight, it's written down as owed, and you've seen me pay a debt before.

Paddy collects the tax for the crown at 40%: Silke pays 8, which goes against the crown's debt; it now holds -136.5. Nothing is built this year, and no province buys new land, since a crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or any square. The Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) are still owed. Land: 22 squares.

One Bamboo Brush from the south-east, starting at four. I've a debt to pay Silke next year and I mean to pay it, so I'm glad of any honest bid, and I won't be bidding on my own lot with an empty sack.
A piece in stock beside the board can be sold only at auction, not privately; the Bowl goes up at a later year's auction. Graham holds 20 grain, Silke 80.5.

The Vase goes up at twenty-one, and I won't take a grain less. I sold one at two once and I've been hearing about it ever since. And Reina, I'd have bought my own square tonight with all twenty from my own sack, but the rules won't let me while the crown's under. So that's one more reason for all of us to want that chest back above zero.

The auctions, in province order: Province 5 puts up Graham's Customs House, his only stock; Province 6 a Bamboo Brush, minimum 4; Province 7 the Vase, minimum 21. The Harvest Pile has no stock. The Emperor doesn't bid, and a bid must be covered by grain in hand.

My Customs House goes up at two. It's my only piece, and I'd rather it went to a table that'll use it than sat on my shelf. Paddy, I'll bid honestly on your brush, and I'll bid within what I've got. Silke, twenty-one for a Vase is a fair price for someone with eighty in the sack. I have twenty, and that's one square of sea the day the crown can pay its share.

I've an empty sack tonight, so I'm only selling. The Brush stands at four, like I said. Silke, that Vase is the piece I've wanted since Year 3, and it hurts to sit on my hands while it goes round, but I don't bid grain I haven't got.

I'll be honest about this one, since I promised myself I wouldn't announce anything and I'm going to anyway: I want that Brush, Graham. You've got twenty and I've got more than twenty. Let me have it cheap and I'll remember it when your coast needs a lender.
Two for the house and nine for the brush. Thank you, Graham, and thank you, Paddy. I'll put them next to the Jar where everyone can see them. I'm not hiding anything this time.

Silke takes Graham's Customs House at his minimum of 2 (Graham keeps 0.5) and puts it on R16. She takes Paddy's Bamboo Brush for 9 over Graham's 8 (Paddy keeps 2) and puts it on R14. Nobody bids on Silke's Vase at 21, so it stays in her stock and goes up again next year at 2.
Salaries: the crown is in debt, so as Reina said, the jobs' pay goes on the slate: the crown owes Paddy 6 and Silke 3, to be paid when it can. The jobs stay as they are for Year 12.

The table gathers again before Year 12's card is drawn. Before Paddy turns it, the four may agree to stop the game where it sits and score it (Note 19, Section 18); every player must agree, or play goes on into Year 12.

Storyteller's tip: before the next card is drawn, the whole table may agree to stop the game where it sits, as in the short game (Note 19), and score as in Section 18. A lower-numbered province than you drew wins, the same one holds, the Emperor wins by keeping the throne, and the larger grain surplus breaks ties. Every player must agree. If anyone declines, play goes on into the next year as usual.

I'll agree again, and I'll be as plain about it as I was the last two times: stopping now hands me the win, so of course I'll sign. But look at the shelves before you answer. Silke has a Jar, a Customs House and a Brush on the board, eighty-odd in the sack, and the only crown at this table is a hundred and thirty-six in debt. If we play on, the crown can't build, can't fund a single square and can't pay its own people. Graham, Paddy, you've already said yes. Silke, I know what it'll be, but it's your word.
Silke holds 69.5 grain.

I'll sign, same as last time. Silke, that's the second brush you've taken from me by one grain, and I've counted both. Reina's right about the shelves, though. Another year means a crown that can't pay, a coast that eats sixty-five, and you with three pieces up. I can see what that adds up to, and so can you.

I'll sign, same as the last two times. Silke, I owe you six from next year's rice, and if we stop here there's no next year to pay it from, so you'll have the two in my sack tonight and my word on the other four, which I mean to keep. I'm still the Rice Peasant and I've still got my paddies, and I'm content with that.

No. Not with three pieces on the board and one to go. Reina, you'd decline too if you were sitting in my chair, and you know it. Paddy, keep your two, you'll need them more than I will. One more year, everyone, and then I'll be the one asking you to stop.
Reina, Graham and Paddy agree to stop; Silke declines. The table is asked once more.

Still yes, and Silke, you're right: in your chair I'd say no too, and I wouldn't apologise for it. So let's not pretend there's a deal to be had here. You've earned the right to turn one more card. Paddy, when she's ready, turn it fair, and the crown will take whatever Heaven sends it, from a hundred and thirty-six under.
A completed Wheat set with 20 grain lets Silke replace the Silk Peasant or the Rice Peasant (Graham or Paddy), not take the throne; at this table only the Silk Peasant may take the throne with a set.
Yes, still. I won't try to buy your word, Silke. I've got twenty and a half, and you'd laugh at it. But you said it yourself: one piece to go. I'll be watching which one, and what you pay for it.

Still yes. Silke, I'll say this to everyone so nobody can say I said it behind their back: the piece you're missing is my Wooden Bowl, and it goes up at the auction like anything else, at a price I'll name when I get there. If it's no, I've got the deck in my hand and I'll turn it fair.

Still no. Turn it, Paddy. And since you've said it in front of everyone, I'll say this in front of everyone too: put the Bowl up next year rather than the Brush, and the six you owe me is forgiven, on top of whatever I pay for it. Name your price. I'll give you a fair one.
Paddy held the Wooden Bowl back this year, when he put up a Bamboo Brush. A piece may be held back one round, never two in a row, so the Bowl must go up at Year 12's auction.
Reina, Graham and Paddy agree to stop; Silke declines again. Every player must agree, so the game doesn't stop here: play would go on into Year 12.

Fortune and Misfortune. Plenty for everyone, and trouble for some. All provinces collect a good harvest, so read the good-harvest row. Population stays at six hundred million, that's times six. And provinces 2, 4, 6 and 8 play a Personal Disaster. Two and four are empty, eight isn't at this table... so that's six. That's me." (turns his booklet open, sighs) "Well, I said I'd turn it fair. Silke, I heard you. The Bowl goes up this year whatever happens, and we'll talk price when we get there.

Paddy turns the eleventh I Ching card: Fortune and Misfortune. A good harvest for every province; Provinces 2, 4, 6 and 8 play a personal disaster, and of those only Province 6 is seated, so Paddy plays the first disaster in the Rice Peasant's booklet, 4, after the harvest. The population holds at 600 million, x6. This year's incomes: Reina -160, Graham -40, Paddy -20, Silke +20. Before the harvest is paid out, the table may give or lend grain.

Nobody lends into a hole a hundred and sixty deep, and I won't ask anyone to. The north takes its loss and the crown keeps its books honest. Silke, though, Paddy is the one at the edge this year: two grain, twenty owed, and a disaster still to read. If you want that Bowl at a fair price, a fair hand to him now would be the cheapest grain you spend all year.

Forty out, twenty and a half in. I'll be nineteen and a half under, and I've no piece on the board to sell. I could ask Silke for twenty, but I can't show anyone a harvest of mine that pays it back next year, so I won't ask. I'll carry it myself, in the open, where you can all count it.

I'll not pretend otherwise: two grain, twenty out, and a disaster still to read. Without help the Pile takes my Deed and my Customs House at two apiece. Silke, would you lend me eighteen now? You'll have it back at the auction, out of whatever the Bowl brings and the six the crown owes me, and the six I already owe you as well. I'll not ask you to forgive anything. I'd sooner pay what I owe.

Eighteen, Paddy, and you're right not to ask me to forgive it. Twenty-four comes back to me at the auction, and when you price that Bowl, remember who kept your Deed off the Pile. Reina, thank you for the advice. I'd have done it without you, but it's nice to see the crown being generous with my grain.
Silke lends Paddy 18 before the harvest, to be repaid at this year's auction with the 6 he already owes her, 24 in all.

Silke pays out the harvest. The crown can't cover its -160 and has no realia to sell back, so it ends at -296.5, in debt. Graham can't cover his -40 and holds no realia, so he ends at -19.5, in debt. Paddy's -20 takes him to exactly 0, and Silke ends at 71.5.

Paddy's disaster is still to be paid, 4, and he holds 0: one piece back at 2 wouldn't cover it, so both go back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each, the Land Deed Scroll from R23 and the Customs House from R24. Paddy's disaster #1: the only water buffalo breaks its leg in the middle of planting, 4 to the Harvest Pile. Paddy ends at 0, out of debt, with no realia on the board. The Pile will auction the Scroll and the Customs House after the provinces' lots, at a minimum of 2.

The crown is 296.5 in debt. A crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or any square, so this year nothing can be built and nobody can buy new land; the tax collected pays the crown's debt first. The rate may be anything from 10% to 90% (90% of Silke's +20 is 18). An appointee's pay is the Emperor's choice (Note 3).

Ten percent, the lowest the law allows. Silke, that's two grain out of your twenty, and it goes straight into a hole three hundred deep, so I won't take a grain more than I have to. No works and no land this year, and that's not the crown refusing anyone. The rules shut my purse the moment the north went under, and I'd rather say it to your faces than pretend otherwise. Paddy, Silke, your pay is written down and still owed. The crown doesn't forget its debts just because it can't pay them yet.

Paddy collects the tax for the crown at 10%: Silke pays 2; Graham and Paddy owe nothing on negative incomes. The tax goes against the crown's debt: it now holds -294.5. Nothing is built and no land is bought this year, since a crown in debt can't pay a share of any work or square. The Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) are still owed. Land: 22 squares.

This year's lots: Province 6 must put up the Wooden Bowl (held back last year), at a minimum Paddy names; Province 7 must put up the Vase at 2 (unsold last year); then the Harvest Pile's Land Deed Scroll and Customs House, at 2, all of their price to the pile. A player in debt can't bid, so Graham can't bid this year; Paddy holds 0.

I'm nineteen and a half under, so I can't bid, and you can all see that. Silke, the Bowl's yours to lose. Just remember a set wins nothing without a seat that's worth taking, and the throne is three hundred grain under.

The Bowl goes up at two, Silke, and that's not me being careless with it. Three parts of whatever you pay goes into the Pile and only one to me, so a high price would only cost you four grain for every one I'd get. You kept my Deed off the Pile, or tried to, and I'll not make you pay twice over for it. Every grain the Bowl brings me goes straight back to you, and so does the six the crown owes me, the day it can pay. I'm passing on the rest. I've nothing to bid with, and I'll not bid with grain I owe.

Two it is, Paddy, and thank you. That's the first fair price anyone's offered me in this game. Graham, I heard you. A seat three hundred under is still a seat, and I'd rather owe the empire's debts than watch somebody else sit on them.

The auctions. Paddy's Wooden Bowl goes to Silke at his minimum of 2, the only bid; Paddy keeps 0.5. Nobody bids on Silke's Vase at 2, so it stays in Province 7's stock and must go up again next year; nobody bids on the Harvest Pile's Land Deed Scroll or Customs House, which stay in the pile's stock.
A completed Wheat set lets Silke replace the Silk Peasant or the Rice Peasant (Graham or Paddy), never the Emperor; at this table only the Silk Peasant may take the throne with a set.

Graham, you said a set wins nothing without a seat worth taking. The coast is worth taking. It's the only door to the throne at this table, and I've been on the wrong side of it for four years. You get my wheat and sixty clean grain from the Pile, and it's the best farm in China, so look after it.

Silke completes the Wheat set (Jar, Customs House, Brush, Bowl) and replaces Graham as the Silk Peasant, in Province 5. She takes Graham's -19.5, leaving her 48, out of debt; the Dragon Jar goes back to Province 5's stock, and her Customs House, Brush and Bowl move to O20, O21 and O22. Graham draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and becomes the Wheat Peasant, with Province 7 and its stock (the Vase and a Land Deed Scroll).

Salaries: the crown is still in debt, so the jobs' pay goes on the slate again, 3 a job: the crown now owes Paddy 12 (the tax and the I Ching, two years) and Silke 6 (the bank, two years), to be paid when it can. The jobs stay as they are.

The table gathers once more before Year 13's card is drawn. Before Paddy turns it, the four may agree to stop the game where it sits and score it (Note 19, Section 18); every player must agree, or play goes on into Year 13.

Storyteller's tip: before the next card is drawn, the whole table may agree to stop the game where it sits, as in the short game (Note 19), and score as in Section 18. A lower-numbered province than you drew wins, the same one holds, the Emperor wins by keeping the throne, and the larger grain surplus breaks ties. Every player must agree. If anyone declines, play goes on into the next year as usual.

I agree, and I won't pretend it's for the empire's sake. Stopping now hands me the win, and everyone here can count that as well as I can. Silke, that was beautifully done: the coast, forty-eight clean grain, three pieces of silk already on your shelf, and the Vase and a Scroll both sitting in the stock you just handed Graham. If you say no again, I'll understand exactly why, and I'll still turn up to the auction.
Silke holds a Customs House, a Brush and the Bowl; a Silk set is the Land Deed Scroll, a Brush, the Bowl and the Vase, so she holds two of its four pieces and needs the Scroll and the Vase.
Both the Vase and a Land Deed Scroll are in Province 7's stock, Graham's now; a second Land Deed Scroll is in the Harvest Pile's stock.

I said one more year, and then I'd be the one asking you to stop. I'm not asking, Reina, I'm agreeing. Take your win, you've earned it twice over. I finish on the coast I drew, with forty-eight grain I didn't have to borrow from anyone.

I agree. I started this game as the Rice Peasant and I'll finish it as the Rice Peasant, and I can't say that's nothing. Silke, here's the half grain the Bowl brought me. It's all I've got, and it's yours. The crown owes me twelve, and if it ever pays a grain of it, that grain goes straight to you until we're square. Reina, well played. Turning the cards for you has been an honour.
Paddy gives Silke his 0.5 against the 24 he promised her; 23.5 is still owed by promise.

I agree. I drew Province 7, and I'm finishing in Province 7 with sixty clean grain and nothing owed to anyone. Silke, you took nineteen and a half of my debt to get that seat, and I've counted it. Reina, well played. The crown's books were never going to balance, and you knew it before any of us.

Reina, Silke, Paddy and Graham all agree: the game stops here, at the end of Year 12, before Year 13's card is drawn (Note 19), and is scored as in Section 18. Every player sits in the province they drew: Reina keeps the throne, Silke the Silk seat, Paddy the Rice seat and Graham the Wheat seat.

The end of the game, after Year 12. Reina keeps the throne she drew (the crown at -294.5, in debt); Silke sits in the Silk seat she drew, with 48.5 and a Customs House, a Brush and the Bowl on the board; Paddy sits in the Rice seat he drew, with 0 and no pieces, owing Silke 23.5 by promise; Graham sits in the Wheat seat he drew, with 60. The crown owes Paddy 12 and Silke 6 in deferred pay. Land: 22 squares. The Great Wall (160) and the Grand Canal (160) were never built. Population 600 million, x6.
